clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder of mitochondrial translation caused by biallelic FARS2 variants, which encode mitochondrial phenylalanyl-tRNA synthetase.
Two broad phenotypes are recognised: a severe early-infantile epileptic (mitochondrial) encephalopathy and a milder later-onset spastic paraplegia designated SPG77.
The encephalopathic form presents with refractory seizures, hypotonia, developmental arrest or regression and frequently lactic acidosis in early infancy.
Blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate are commonly raised, reflecting a combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency (combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 14).
Muscle or fibroblast studies may show a combined deficiency of several respiratory chain complexes rather than an isolated single-complex defect.
Brain MRI often shows progressive cerebral atrophy with variable white-matter, thalamic or brainstem signal change.
The SPG77 phenotype presents in childhood with slowly progressive lower-limb spasticity, sometimes with ataxia and milder cognitive involvement.
Diagnosis rests on molecular genetic testing; enzyme, biochemical and imaging findings are supportive but non-specific.
reference.pathophysiology: FARS2 on chromosome 6p25.1 encodes the mitochondrial phenylalanyl-tRNA synthetase (mtPheRS), a nuclear-encoded enzyme imported into the mitochondrion where it charges (aminoacylates) mitochondrial tRNA-Phe with phenylalanine, an obligatory step in mitochondrial protein synthesis. Because the mitochondrial ribosome translates the thirteen mtDNA-encoded subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation machinery, biallelic loss-of-function or hypomorphic FARS2 variants impair mitochondrial translation and produce a combined deficiency of multiple respiratory chain complexes (combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 14). The resulting bioenergetic failure is most damaging to the highly metabolically active developing brain, giving rise either to a devastating neonatal or early-infantile epileptic encephalopathy with lactic acidosis, or, where residual enzyme activity is greater, to a comparatively mild childhood-onset spastic paraplegia (SPG77).
additionalDifferentials: Other mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase disorders (for example AARS2, EARS2, DARS2, RARS2, NARS2)
Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome and other POLG-related disorders
Leigh syndrome and Leigh-like disease from other causes
Other early-infantile epileptic and developmental encephalopathies
For the SPG77 phenotype, other hereditary spastic paraplegias
Neonatal or infantile mitochondrial encephalomyopathies with lactic acidosis
additionalInvestigations: Blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate with paired pyruvate
Plasma amino acids and urine organic acids
Electroencephalography, which may show an epileptic encephalopathy pattern
Muscle biopsy with respiratory chain (complex) enzyme assays
Molecular genetic testing (FARS2 sequencing, gene panel or exome)
Fibroblast studies of mitochondrial translation where available
reference.prognosis: The early-infantile epileptic encephalopathy carries a poor prognosis, often with death in infancy or early childhood. The SPG77 phenotype is slowly progressive and compatible with prolonged survival.
pitfalls: A normal lactate does not exclude the diagnosis.
The wide phenotypic spectrum, from severe encephalopathy to SPG77, leads to under-recognition.
The spastic paraplegia phenotype can be mislabelled as cerebral palsy.
Imaging and enzyme findings overlap with other mitochondrial disorders, so genetic confirmation is essential.
references: Peer-reviewed reviews of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase disorders
management: Control refractory seizures with antiseizure medications, generally avoiding sodium valproate because of the mitochondrial hepatotoxicity risk
Provide supportive metabolic care including management of lactic acidosis and consideration of a mitochondrial vitamin and cofactor cocktail
Manage spasticity in the SPG77 phenotype with antispasticity agents such as baclofen alongside physiotherapy and orthoses
Support development, nutrition, feeding and respiratory function through multidisciplinary rehabilitation
Involve neurology, metabolic medicine and palliative care given the poor prognosis of the early-infantile encephalopathic form
Offer genetic counselling and family testing given autosomal recessive FARS2 inheritance
